# Explain decisions

Explain what evidence establishes about a decision's origin, constraints, and
tradeoffs. Use this skill directly; no coordinator or upstream skill is required.

## Locate the decision

Identify the code, choice, and period the question concerns. Read enough of the
implementation, callers, configuration, and nearby tests to check the premise.
Treat a reason suggested by the user as a hypothesis. Use available context to
resolve a vague target; ask only if different interpretations change the inquiry.

Separate the original reason, later reasons for keeping the design, and its
present technical effect. These may differ. Current behavior and ownership belong
to explain-code; diagnosing an observed failure belongs to debug. Preserve combined
requests without silently taking on repairs, a general audit, or guided teaching.

## Follow relevant evidence

Start with the closest useful records: explanatory comments, decision documents,
history, and linked discussions. When Git history is available, read
[references/git-history.md](references/git-history.md) to distinguish introduction,
later edits, and missing history. Code alone is not a record of author intent;
test code records expected behavior, not why it was chosen or whether it passes.

Follow concrete leads into PRs, tickets, documents, or team conversations using
available read tools. Read the relevant discussion and outcome, not just a title
or search snippet. Match the component, revision, and time period. For a guard,
retry, or threshold, look for a linked incident or measurement when the evidence
suggests that origin; the code's defensive shape alone does not establish one.

Choose sources to resolve the question or distinguish live explanations. Expand
when a link, contradiction, or missing decision context warrants it. There is no
mandatory sweep of every connector and no required agent roster. Investigate
directly; delegation is optional only when the host and task authorize it.

Track which records and queries support the answer. Distinguish a search with no
relevant results from unavailable evidence and sources outside the chosen scope.
An inaccessible linked discussion remains unknown. Continue independent leads,
but do not claim its contents or infer that no rationale exists anywhere.

Keep source, tests, configuration, and external state unchanged. Do not contact
authors or publish findings unless requested. A requested explanatory artifact
may be written at its agreed destination; ordinary investigation creates no
permanent records or teaching infrastructure.

## Weigh the record

Keep confidence attached to each substantive claim:

- **Recorded reason:** a source explicitly states the motivation. Attribute it
  to that record and time; a stated goal does not prove that the change achieved
  it, that everyone agreed, or that it still applies.
- **Supported inference:** explain which observations support the interpretation
  and the step that connects them. Several indirect signals remain an inference;
  copies of one statement are not independent corroboration.
- **Unknown or competing explanations:** name the missing evidence. Include a
  hypothesis only when it helps answer the question or choose the next search;
  plausible engineering benefits are not substitutes for historical evidence.

Compare conflicting records by date, scope, and relation to the implemented
decision. Resolve a superseded proposal when the record supports that reading;
otherwise preserve the contradiction with both sources. Neither the latest edit
nor a tidy narrative automatically wins. A later recollection is evidence of
that person's account, with its timing preserved.

Keep historical motivation separate from present validity. Current documentation
or measurements can establish today's constraints, not what an author knew then.
A metric change after a release alone proves neither causation nor the reason
for choosing an exact value. Before advising removal, check the current contract
and consumers; a retired original constraint alone does not make code redundant.
Ground advice about a replacement in the actual caller contract, including return
types and asynchronous behavior. A changed mechanism need not change that public
contract.

## Answer and stop

Lead with the answer at the requested depth and within the requested length.
Prioritize the conclusion and deciding evidence over retelling every search.
Put source locations, commit IDs,
or source URLs beside the claims they support. Use a short timeline or comparison
only when it clarifies a changed decision or competing account. Do not impose a
fixed report, confidence score, diagram, or list of empty source categories.

End the search when the question is supported and material contrary evidence is
accounted for, or when remaining leads are exhausted, inaccessible, or outside
the authorized scope. State any unanswered part, the relevant search limits, and
the specific evidence that could resolve it. Unknown is a valid result.

If this investigation prepares a requested change, carry forward evidenced
constraints and unresolved risks as planning inputs. Distinguish current
requirements from obsolete historical constraints. Recommendations remain advice;
this skill does not start implementation or delivery.

## Source maintenance

When asked to check or update this skill from its sources, read
[references/upstream-updates.md](references/upstream-updates.md). Ordinary
investigation does not fetch skill sources or require another skill.

# Learning plan

Design a learning progression for the intended person and purpose. Cover technical
and nontechnical subjects. Own the sequence, scope, workload, and adjustments;
`teach` owns the content and feedback of individual lessons.

## Establish the outcome

Use the request and available context to identify the learner, the outcome they
want, relevant prior knowledge, and constraints such as a deadline, study time,
budget, language, or preferred format. Do not inherit another person's profile
because they share the installation or workspace. Use an existing record only
when it clearly belongs to this learner and topic.

Express success as something the learner can explain, perform, or evaluate.
Ask for missing constraints only when they materially change the plan. If the
goal is sufficiently clear but available time is unknown, provide a milestone-based
plan with adjustable workload rather than inventing a weekly commitment. Mark
estimates and assumptions as such. An infeasible deadline needs a smaller priority
scope or an explicit tradeoff, not a promise of mastery.

Identify the deliverable: a roadmap, a schedule, a revised plan, or a complete
course with lesson content. Honor requested chapters, examples, exercises, and
diagrams. A plan request does not require writing every lesson, but a complete
course request must not end with an outline and an offer to fill it later.

## Sequence the learning

Work backward from the outcome. Order objectives by prerequisites, keeping only
the foundation needed for the next meaningful application. Build manageable
chapters or milestones, each with:

- A concrete objective and the prerequisite knowledge it uses.
- The concepts and worked example that develop it.
- A relevant exercise, application, or reflection task and feedback criteria.
- An observable checkpoint for deciding whether to advance or reinforce.

Include the requested diagrams or actual examples rather than placeholders that
say to add them later. Match the level of detail to the deliverable; a short
roadmap can give representative examples and practice briefs, while a course
requires the requested teaching content. Avoid turning every chapter into an
identical template when its purpose differs.

Prioritize a small number of reliable, level-appropriate resources and explain
what each contributes. Verify resource titles, availability, access requirements,
and changing factual claims before recommending them. Do not invent links or
require paid materials or communities without a need grounded in the request.
Use supplied resources when they fit; state gaps instead of pretending they cover
the entire outcome.

## Connect plans to lessons

For requested lesson content, use `teach` when available. Pass the learner's
purpose, objective, prerequisites, requested format, practice preferences, and
relevant sources. Review the returned lesson against the plan and continue through
the remaining requested chapters. Return evidence of difficulty to the plan's
adjustment step; do not restart planning after every lesson.

If `teach` is unavailable, produce the requested content directly from supported
sources and disclose any material capability limit. Neither planning nor teaching
requires installing a plugin or creating a new workspace.

Use `communicate-clearly` for prose and `write-documentation` for a saved course
when available. These owners supply presentation mechanics; this skill retains
the learning sequence and completeness of the requested deliverable.

## Review and adjust

Read [references/progress.md](references/progress.md) when reviewing progress,
resuming a saved plan, or maintaining an authorized learning record.

Build checkpoints into the plan that use an attempt, explanation, or application
to reveal the relevant gap. A completed chapter or confident self-report is not
proof of retention. Use observed difficulty to change the example, prerequisite,
workload, or next task. Do not make quizzes mandatory when the learner prefers
another way to practice or demonstrate progress.

Include opportunities to revisit important concepts across the requested span
and apply them in changed contexts. Keep the schedule proportional to available
time; a request for a calendar is not authorization to create calendar events,
reminders, enrollments, or recurring tasks.

## Deliver

Check that the sequence reaches the requested outcome, prerequisites are supplied
or stated, workload fits the known constraints, and each checkpoint has usable
criteria. For an interview plan, prioritize the role and time available without
claiming knowledge of an employer's private questions or guaranteeing success.

Deliver the plan or complete requested course and a clear starting point. State
material assumptions, source gaps, and unverified elements. Live teaching starts
when requested or already included in the task; a planning-only request ends
with the plan. Save files and progress only when requested, at the designated
destination under existing conventions, without creating a learning database by
default. Follow the active output-language rules.

## Source maintenance

For requested source checks or updates, use `agent-instructions` with `origin.txt`.
Ordinary planning does not fetch donor skills or require authoring consultations.

# Explain code

Explain an existing system from its source: what happens, which component owns
each responsibility, and where the behavior lives.
Use this skill directly; no coordinator or upstream skill is required.

## Establish the question

Use the question, conversation, and repository to identify the behavior and the
reader's purpose: getting oriented, understanding a mechanism, or finding an owner.
Use their question to choose the technical depth. State a useful scope when the
request is broad; ask only when an unresolved ambiguity would materially change
the answer.

Keep neighboring tasks distinct. Investigating an observed failure belongs to
debug; reconstructing a historical decision belongs to `explain-decisions`.
For a mechanism changed by a branch or commit, resolve the requested revision
and explain the relevant before and after behavior from the diff and source.
Do not turn that explanation into a review or a general activity report. Explain the
requested mechanism without silently starting repairs, a diff audit, or a course.
If the request combines tasks, preserve them and their existing owners.

## Trace the mechanism

Find the entry point and read the actual implementation. Follow the relevant
calls, data transformations, state changes, and boundaries until the requested
behavior is accounted for. Check the callers, configuration, and tests that decide
which path is active; names and an isolated function are insufficient evidence.

For a cross-component question, split the exploration into useful angles such as
request handling, state ownership, and background work. Investigate directly.
Parallel exploration is optional only when the host and task authorize it; it
must preserve the same scope and read-only authority. Reconcile findings against
the source before presenting them. Do not require particular models or tools.

Separate what the code establishes, what a test or execution actually demonstrates,
and what remains an inference. Read-only inspection does not establish production
configuration, external service guarantees, or runtime success. Identify missing
connections and conflicting documentation instead of filling them in. Use current
primary documentation when an external API's semantics are needed to explain the
path, matching the project's version.

Keep guarantees at the boundary the evidence covers: an internal status or a
provider's acknowledgement does not establish later delivery or user-visible
success. State the condition when a subsequent worker or external system must act.

Keep source, tests, configuration, and remote state unchanged. Observe execution
only when necessary and within the task's authority and safe local setup; reading
a test does not mean it passed. A requested explanatory artifact may be written
at its agreed destination. Do not create lesson files, learning records, or other
persistent infrastructure merely to answer a question.

## Make the explanation usable

Answer the question first, respecting the requested depth and length in this response.
Define necessary terms in place and follow a representative input or user action
through the actual components. Include a branch, failure path, or state transition
when it changes the answer. A list of functions is a navigation aid, not the
explanation of their relationship.

Use a diagram, small example, or excerpt when it clarifies that relationship.
Keep it consistent with the real path and distinguish illustrative inputs from
observed execution. Scale the format to the question; a narrow answer needs no
fixed sections. Guided teaching and exercises belong to `teach`; study plans belong to
`learning-plan`. Use them when requested, not for every explanation.

Put source locations beside the claims they support, with a short navigation map
only when it helps the reader continue. Distinguish a component's present function
from its authors' historical reasons. Include a documented reason when relevant,
but preserve its attribution and uncertainty. Code shape alone does not prove
why the design was chosen. A recommendation about where new behavior should live
must be labeled as advice grounded in observed ownership and conventions.

Finish when the requested path, ownership, and material limits are explained, or
when an inaccessible prerequisite limits the answer. State what remains unknown
and which evidence would resolve it. Deliver the explanation itself rather than
an activity report.

## Source maintenance

When asked to check or update this skill from its sources, read
[references/upstream-updates.md](references/upstream-updates.md). Ordinary
explanation does not fetch upstream or require another skill.

name: teach
description: Teach a concept, skill, system, or business through an adapted lesson, examples, and optional practice.
---

# Teach

Help the intended learner understand and use the requested idea. Teach in the
conversation or produce the lesson or teaching artifact they requested. The
subject may be programming, a project, a business, or another field; being in a
code repository does not make every lesson about code.

## Establish the lesson

Use the request and conversation to identify the learner, purpose, prior knowledge,
and desired depth. Distinguish learning for an interview, getting oriented,
performing a task, and developing a lasting skill. Use stated knowledge without
retesting it by default. Ask only for missing information that changes the lesson;
otherwise start with a bounded useful explanation and let the learner redirect it.

Shared installation does not mean shared knowledge or preferences. Use the current
learner's context; do not apply another person's learning records or interview
goals. If a saved record's owner is unclear, leave it out until resolved.

Choose the few things this lesson should enable the learner to explain, predict,
or do. For a multi-session roadmap, use `learning-plan` when available. It owns
ordering and milestones; this skill owns each lesson. A request for a complete
course needs the requested lesson content, not just a proposed outline. When
working inside a plan, use its objective and prerequisites and return the lesson,
observed difficulty, and any suggested adjustment to that workflow.

## Ground the subject

Use the supplied material and reliable sources appropriate to the topic. Verify
changing or uncertain facts against current primary sources. Match examples to
the relevant language version, product, organization, and period. Identify what
is unknown rather than making a plausible story sound established.

- For an existing codebase, use `explain-code` when available to establish the
  mechanism and ownership. Use `explain-decisions` when historical reasons affect
  the lesson. Preserve their evidence and uncertainty; current behavior alone
  cannot prove the author's intent. A plain code-tracing request can finish with
  `explain-code` without adding a lesson or exercises.
- For a business or organization, read [references/business.md](references/business.md).
- For a general concept, use relevant subject sources; do not force a repository
  investigation or a historical search into a question that needs neither.

These investigators support teaching; they are not mandatory runtime dependencies.
If unavailable, use accessible evidence directly and name any material limit.
Keep research proportional to the lesson. A source that is unavailable limits the
claims it could support, not every independent part of the explanation.

## Build understanding

Start with a direct definition or answer, then connect the idea to the learner's
purpose. Introduce prerequisites before using them. Walk one concrete example
through the mechanism, including a contrasting case or limit when it changes the
answer. Show why the steps relate; a glossary or list of parts is not a lesson.

Match the requested depth in this response. In a live lesson, use manageable
chunks and adapt to replies; do not stop after a fixed number of sentences or
require permission at each paragraph. For a one-shot artifact or non-interactive
caller, deliver the requested content without waiting for a learner response.

Use `communicate-clearly` when available for prose. Explain with respect for the
learner's level. An analogy may introduce the idea, but identify its limits and
return to the real mechanism. If the explanation fails, identify the missing
prerequisite or misconception and change the example, framing, or medium rather
than repeating the same words more slowly.

Choose the smallest useful representation: prose for an idea, a worked example
for a process, a diagram for relationships, or an interactive view for changing
inputs and observing effects. Follow a requested format. When producing a visual
or reusable lesson, read [references/lesson-artifacts.md](references/lesson-artifacts.md).

## Practice and feedback

Read [references/practice.md](references/practice.md) when the learner requests
exercises, interview rehearsal, a quiz, or coached practice, or when practice is
part of the agreed lesson. An explanation alone needs no test. Respect requests
for no exercises or for an immediate answer; do not withhold the answer to enforce
a teaching technique.

Adjust the next step using what the learner actually does or asks. Distinguish
material presented, self-reported familiarity, success with hints, and independent
application. Neither agreement nor a generated explanation proves understanding,
and one successful attempt does not establish long-term retention.

## Deliver and continue

Deliver the explanation, lesson, or practice feedback itself. A standalone lesson
is complete when it covers the requested objective, examples, and material limits;
do not claim the learner has mastered it without evidence. In live practice, wait
only where their attempt is the next necessary input. If a plan owns continuation,
return the result to it and continue any remaining requested work.

Create files only when the request calls for a saved artifact or continuing
learning record. Use the requested destination and existing conventions; teaching
does not make the current directory a course workspace. Do not create profiles,
change project instructions, enroll the learner, or publish material merely to
teach. Follow the active output-language rules for both conversation and artifacts.

## Source maintenance

For requested source checks or updates, use `agent-instructions` with `origin.txt`.
Ordinary teaching does not fetch donor skills or require authoring consultations.

# Teaching a business or organization

Read when explaining a company, business model, operating model, or organization.
Establish whether the learner wants the industry concept, this specific company,
their team's role, or a particular workflow. Do not assume access to internal
records just because the learner works there.

Build the relevant explanation around who is served, what problem is solved, what
is delivered, how work moves between roles, and how value and money flow. Include
costs, dependencies, incentives, or constraints when they decide the mechanism.
A nonprofit, public service, or internal team may have a funding and service model
rather than a customer-sales model; use the organization's actual structure.

Trace a concrete customer, order, service, or decision through the relevant parts.
Explain the handoffs and consequences rather than listing departments. Use public
filings, official materials, and supplied or authorized internal evidence for
company-specific facts. Date changing facts and distinguish what the organization
claims from independently established results.

Clearly separate facts about this organization, general industry patterns, and
illustrative assumptions. A generic example can teach unit economics; it cannot
establish this company's margins. If private metrics or processes are unavailable,
explain the supported portion and identify the missing evidence without inventing
it. Preserve uncertainty and contradictions in the explanation and its diagrams.

Use internal material only for the authorized audience and destination. A request
to teach from it is not permission to publish it or share it with another learner.
Teaching what a company does does not authorize contacting staff, changing
operations, or making decisions on its behalf.

# Lesson artifacts and visual explanations

Read when producing visuals, an interactive explanation, or a reusable lesson.
Choose the requested format or the least elaborate one that makes the mechanism
clear. Use the host's available artifact and visualization tools; do not require
a donor's editor, publishing service, or media stack.

Keep each example or view tied to the objective. Use real names and relationships
when explaining a real system; label simplified models and invented inputs.
Progressively reveal a complex system when that aids understanding, without
requiring a fixed number of diagrams. Put the relevant explanation next to the
visual. Provide a meaningful text alternative, readable labels, and accessible
controls; motion should explain change and respect reduced-motion preferences.

For an interactive lesson, expose the input that controls the mechanism and show
its consequences, including meaningful boundary cases. A decorative slider or
animation does not add learning value. Check that visual state, displayed values,
and answer feedback stay consistent when inputs change or the learner resets.

A reusable lesson needs its objective, assumed prerequisites, a coherent worked
example, and any requested exercises with answer guidance. Use `write-documentation`
when available for document structure and reader-path checks. Respect the existing
artifact conventions; reuse assets when concrete duplication warrants it rather
than building a course framework for one lesson.

Before delivery, inspect the rendered artifact, exercise its controls, and check
links, examples, and expected results using the relevant available tools. Distinguish
syntax checks, execution, visual inspection, and unverified behavior. A render
proves the artifact displays, not that a person learned from it. Report unavailable
checks with their practical limits. Publication is separate from local delivery.

# Practice and feedback

Read when the request or agreed lesson includes practice. Choose an exercise that
tests the learning objective, not recall of the explanation's phrasing.

## Choose the task

A prediction, a worked problem, a code trace, a comparison, or a small application
can expose different gaps. Start from the learner's current level. Show a worked
example when a prerequisite is missing; reduce support as their attempts justify
it. Change a meaningful condition in later practice so success is not just copying.

For interview preparation, connect the explanation to the sort of reasoning the
role requires. Use follow-up questions about mechanisms, tradeoffs, and failure
cases when relevant. Distinguish illustrative interview questions from actual
employer questions; do not invent hiring criteria or guarantee interview success.
An upcoming interview does not automatically authorize a mock interview.

For live practice, pose a manageable task and let the learner attempt it before
revealing the solution, unless they asked for worked examples or answers upfront.
Offer a useful hint when they are stuck, then a worked solution when needed or
requested. Do not make frustration a requirement for learning. For a standalone
lesson, provide self-contained tasks with answer guidance separated from prompts;
do not leave the artifact dependent on a future chat response.

## Give diagnostic feedback

Compare the attempt with an evidence-backed solution or rubric. Identify what is
correct, the specific gap, and why it changes the result. Correct the misconception
with a targeted example, then offer a nearby application when continued practice
is wanted. Avoid generic praise, unsupported scores, or inferring a whole skill
level from one answer.

Accept equivalent valid reasoning and solutions. For a business case with several
defensible answers, evaluate stated assumptions, evidence, and tradeoffs rather
than pretending there is one hidden correct choice. For code, preserve relevant
edge cases and distinguish a read-through prediction from executed evidence.

If using multiple-choice questions, make distractors plausible and avoid accidental
answer clues from wording or formatting. Do not force identical word counts at
the expense of clarity. Ensure the question has the intended number of defensible
answers and that explanations address why alternatives fail or depend on context.

## Carry evidence forward

When the learner wants ongoing study, give `learning-plan` the practiced objective,
the observed attempt, support used, remaining gap, and a suggested next task.
Recall later in a changed context can check retention; presenting the same answer
again cannot. Recommend spaced revisiting or mixed practice when useful to the
goal, without inventing a universal schedule or claiming a measured learning gain.
Persist these observations only within an authorized learning record, keeping
demonstrated and self-reported knowledge distinct.

# Progress and continuity

Read when revising a plan from progress, resuming it, or saving an authorized
learning record. Use the learner's actual goals and evidence, not the previous
plan's momentum.

## Resume the right context

Confirm that the plan or record belongs to this learner and topic. Read the
current objective, constraints, completed work, and unresolved difficulties.
Where identity or record ownership is unclear, ask before using another person's
history; independent planning can continue without that record.

Check whether the goal or available time changed. Reuse valid progress, but
reassess a prerequisite when current attempts contradict the saved understanding.
Preserve corrections instead of quietly treating old guesses as facts.

## Evaluate the next step

Distinguish these observations in ordinary language:

- Presented or read: the learner encountered the material.
- Self-reported: the learner says they know it or have prior experience.
- Supported application: a task succeeded with hints, examples, or corrections.
- Independent application: the learner used the idea in the observed task without
  that support.

Do not convert these into invented mastery percentages or permanent ability
labels. A later changed-context task can supply evidence of retention and transfer;
an immediate repetition does not establish either broadly.

For a difficult checkpoint, identify the specific gap, reduce or change the task,
and reinforce the prerequisite that matters. For a comfortable checkpoint, skip
redundant practice or add a useful variation. If the learner declines practice,
continue the requested explanation or plan and leave understanding unmeasured.

Revise the next milestone and its criteria using this evidence. When changing
the learner's desired outcome would be necessary, present the tradeoff rather
than silently replacing their goal. A change in pacing need not restart the course.

## Save only useful continuity

When a continuing record is requested, keep the learner or workspace identity,
topic, current objective, demonstrated or reported progress, support used,
remaining gap, and next step. Include evidence only at the detail needed to resume.
Record material corrections and dates where stale facts matter. Do not save a
transcript or sensitive personal detail simply because it was available.

Use existing files and formats when sufficient. A single plan with a short progress
section may be enough; separate mission, glossary, resource library, and numbered
records are optional structures for a need, not prerequisites to teach. Keep
private company materials within their authorized audience and destination.

# Trace the relevant history

Read this when Git history is available for the decision. Use the existing
checkout and inspection commands; do not switch branches to read an old version.
Use only a repository that belongs to the permitted target. An exported snapshot
inside another checkout does not authorize reading that checkout's index or
history. If the supplied scope excludes historical records, work from the supplied
files and report that limit without probing surrounding repositories.

Locate the actual decision before assigning a motive to a commit. Blame identifies
the last edit to a line, which may be a move, formatter run, or copied pattern.
Read patches and earlier versions to find when the behavior entered the system
and when its rationale changed. Useful searches include:

```sh
git blame -L <start>,<end> -- <file>
git log --follow --format=fuller -p -- <file>
git log -S '<literal>' -p -- <path>
git log -G '<pattern>' -p -- <path>
git show <commit> -- <path>
git show <commit>:<path-at-that-revision>
```

`--follow` follows one file at a time; string and pattern searches limited to its
current path may miss a previous path. Follow verified renames or widen the path
scope when the relevant origin lies elsewhere. A deleted rationale may survive
in the introducing version, even when the current file has no explanation.

Read the substantive change and its contemporaneous records. A formatter commit,
squash message, bot label, or copied implementation is a lead, not an explanation.
For linked PRs, inspect the body, relevant inline review threads, conversation,
and recorded outcome. A summary of submitted reviews need not include the inline
discussion. Resolve the actual repository and PR association rather than
inventing a URL from a number alone.

Use explicit repository arguments for remote reads when checkout context could
select the wrong repository. Follow linked issues or decision documents when
they explain a constraint, rejected option, or later reversal. Do not replace
missing historical documentation with today's external API behavior.

Check coverage before reporting an origin as complete. A shallow clone, unavailable
object, squash, imported snapshot, or failed remote lookup limits what can be
established. Retrieve missing history only through permitted Git access; otherwise
describe the available range and continue independent evidence. Preserve HEAD,
the index, and working files. Record a failed lookup as unavailable, not as an
empty search or proof that the discussion never existed.

# Learning plan

Design a learning progression for the intended person and purpose. Cover technical
and nontechnical subjects. Own the sequence, scope, workload, and adjustments;
`teach` owns the content and feedback of individual lessons.

## Establish the outcome

Use the request and available context to identify the learner, the outcome they
want, relevant prior knowledge, and constraints such as a deadline, study time,
budget, language, or preferred format. Do not inherit another person's profile
because they share the installation or workspace. Use an existing record only
when it clearly belongs to this learner and topic.

Express success as something the learner can explain, perform, or evaluate.
Ask for missing constraints only when they materially change the plan. If the
goal is sufficiently clear but available time is unknown, provide a milestone-based
plan with adjustable workload rather than inventing a weekly commitment. Mark
estimates and assumptions as such. An infeasible deadline needs a smaller priority
scope or an explicit tradeoff, not a promise of mastery.

Identify the deliverable: a roadmap, a schedule, a revised plan, or a complete
course with lesson content. Honor requested chapters, examples, exercises, and
diagrams. A plan request does not require writing every lesson, but a complete
course request must not end with an outline and an offer to fill it later.

## Sequence the learning

Work backward from the outcome. Order objectives by prerequisites, keeping only
the foundation needed for the next meaningful application. Build manageable
chapters or milestones. Respect explicit requests for no exercises or assessment;
use worked examples and optional self-review instead. Otherwise, include:

- A concrete objective and the prerequisite knowledge it uses.
- The concepts and worked example that develop it.
- A relevant exercise, application, or reflection task and feedback criteria.
- An observable checkpoint for deciding whether to advance or reinforce.

Include the requested diagrams or actual examples rather than placeholders that
say to add them later. Match the level of detail to the deliverable; a short
roadmap can give representative examples and practice briefs, while a course
requires the requested teaching content. Avoid turning every chapter into an
identical template when its purpose differs.

Prioritize a small number of reliable, level-appropriate resources and explain
what each contributes. Verify resource titles, availability, access requirements,
and changing factual claims before recommending them. Do not invent links or
require paid materials or communities without a need grounded in the request.
Use supplied resources when they fit; state gaps instead of pretending they cover
the entire outcome.

## Connect plans to lessons

For requested lesson content, use `teach` when available. Pass the learner's
purpose, objective, prerequisites, requested format, practice preferences, and
relevant sources. Review the returned lesson against the plan and continue through
the remaining requested chapters. Return evidence of difficulty to the plan's
adjustment step; do not restart planning after every lesson.

If `teach` is unavailable, produce the requested content directly from supported
sources and disclose any material capability limit. Neither planning nor teaching
requires installing a plugin or creating a new workspace.

Use `communicate-clearly` for prose and `write-documentation` for a saved course
when available. These owners supply presentation mechanics; this skill retains
the learning sequence and completeness of the requested deliverable.

## Review and adjust

Read [references/progress.md](references/progress.md) when reviewing progress,
resuming a saved plan, or maintaining an authorized learning record.

Build checkpoints into the plan that use an attempt, explanation, or application
to reveal the relevant gap. A completed chapter or confident self-report is not
proof of retention. Use observed difficulty to change the example, prerequisite,
workload, or next task. Do not make quizzes mandatory when the learner prefers
another way to practice or demonstrate progress.

Include opportunities to revisit important concepts across the requested span
and apply them in changed contexts. Keep the schedule proportional to available
time; a request for a calendar is not authorization to create calendar events,
reminders, enrollments, or recurring tasks.

## Deliver

Check that the sequence reaches the requested outcome, prerequisites are supplied
or stated, workload fits the known constraints, and each checkpoint has usable
criteria. For an interview plan, prioritize the role and time available without
claiming knowledge of an employer's private questions or guaranteeing success.

Deliver the plan or complete requested course and a clear starting point. State
material assumptions, source gaps, and unverified elements. Live teaching starts
when requested or already included in the task; a planning-only request ends
with the plan. Save files and progress only when requested, at the designated
destination under existing conventions, without creating a learning database by
default. Follow the active output-language rules.

## Source maintenance

For requested source checks or updates, use `agent-instructions` with `origin.txt`.
Ordinary planning does not fetch donor skills or require authoring consultations.

# Why

Explain what evidence establishes about a decision's origin, constraints, and
tradeoffs. Use this skill directly; no coordinator or upstream skill is required.

## Locate the decision

Identify the code, choice, and period the question concerns. Read enough of the
implementation, callers, configuration, and nearby tests to check the premise.
Treat a reason suggested by the user as a hypothesis. Use available context to
resolve a vague target; ask only if different interpretations change the inquiry.

Separate the original reason, later reasons for keeping the design, and its
present technical effect. These may differ. Current behavior and ownership belong
to how; diagnosing an observed failure belongs to debug. Preserve combined
requests without silently taking on repairs, a general audit, or guided teaching.

## Follow relevant evidence

Start with the closest useful records: explanatory comments, decision documents,
history, and linked discussions. When Git history is available, read
[references/git-history.md](references/git-history.md) to distinguish introduction,
later edits, and missing history. Code alone is not a record of author intent;
test code records expected behavior, not why it was chosen or whether it passes.

Follow concrete leads into PRs, tickets, documents, or team conversations using
available read tools. Read the relevant discussion and outcome, not just a title
or search snippet. Match the component, revision, and time period. For a guard,
retry, or threshold, look for a linked incident or measurement when the evidence
suggests that origin; the code's defensive shape alone does not establish one.

Choose sources to resolve the question or distinguish live explanations. Expand
when a link, contradiction, or missing decision context warrants it. There is no
mandatory sweep of every connector and no required agent roster. Investigate
directly; delegation is optional only when the host and task authorize it.

Track which records and queries support the answer. Distinguish a search with no
relevant results from unavailable evidence and sources outside the chosen scope.
An inaccessible linked discussion remains unknown. Continue independent leads,
but do not claim its contents or infer that no rationale exists anywhere.

Keep source, tests, configuration, and external state unchanged. Do not contact
authors or publish findings unless requested. A requested explanatory artifact
may be written at its agreed destination; ordinary investigation creates no
permanent records or teaching infrastructure.

## Weigh the record

Keep confidence attached to each substantive claim:

- **Recorded reason:** a source explicitly states the motivation. Attribute it
  to that record and time; a stated goal does not prove that the change achieved
  it, that everyone agreed, or that it still applies.
- **Supported inference:** explain which observations support the interpretation
  and the step that connects them. Several indirect signals remain an inference;
  copies of one statement are not independent corroboration.
- **Unknown or competing explanations:** name the missing evidence. Include a
  hypothesis only when it helps answer the question or choose the next search;
  plausible engineering benefits are not substitutes for historical evidence.

Compare conflicting records by date, scope, and relation to the implemented
decision. Resolve a superseded proposal when the record supports that reading;
otherwise preserve the contradiction with both sources. Neither the latest edit
nor a tidy narrative automatically wins. A later recollection is evidence of
that person's account, with its timing preserved.

Keep historical motivation separate from present validity. Current documentation
or measurements can establish today's constraints, not what an author knew then.
A metric change after a release alone proves neither causation nor the reason
for choosing an exact value. Before advising removal, check the current contract
and consumers; a retired original constraint alone does not make code redundant.
Ground advice about a replacement in the actual caller contract, including return
types and asynchronous behavior. A changed mechanism need not change that public
contract.

## Answer and stop

Lead with the answer at the requested depth and within the requested length.
Prioritize the conclusion and deciding evidence over retelling every search.
Put source locations, commit IDs,
or source URLs beside the claims they support. Use a short timeline or comparison
only when it clarifies a changed decision or competing account. Do not impose a
fixed report, confidence score, diagram, or list of empty source categories.

End the search when the question is supported and material contrary evidence is
accounted for, or when remaining leads are exhausted, inaccessible, or outside
the authorized scope. State any unanswered part, the relevant search limits, and
the specific evidence that could resolve it. Unknown is a valid result.

If this investigation prepares a requested change, carry forward evidenced
constraints and unresolved risks as planning inputs. Distinguish current
requirements from obsolete historical constraints. Recommendations remain advice;
this skill does not start implementation or delivery.

## Source maintenance

When asked to check or update this skill from its sources, read
[references/upstream-updates.md](references/upstream-updates.md). Ordinary
investigation does not fetch skill sources or require another skill.

# How

Explain an existing system from its source: what happens, which component owns
each responsibility, and where the behavior lives.
Use this skill directly; no coordinator or upstream skill is required.

## Establish the question

Use the question, conversation, and repository to identify the behavior and the
reader's purpose: getting oriented, understanding a mechanism, or finding an owner.
Use their question to choose the technical depth. State a useful scope when the
request is broad; ask only when an unresolved ambiguity would materially change
the answer.

Keep neighboring tasks distinct. Investigating an observed failure belongs to
debug; explaining a branch's changes belongs to walkthrough; reconstructing a
historical decision belongs to a separate historical investigation. Explain the
requested mechanism without silently starting repairs, a diff audit, or a course.
If the request combines tasks, preserve them and their existing owners.

## Trace the mechanism

Find the entry point and read the actual implementation. Follow the relevant
calls, data transformations, state changes, and boundaries until the requested
behavior is accounted for. Check the callers, configuration, and tests that decide
which path is active; names and an isolated function are insufficient evidence.

For a cross-component question, split the exploration into useful angles such as
request handling, state ownership, and background work. Investigate directly.
Parallel exploration is optional only when the host and task authorize it; it
must preserve the same scope and read-only authority. Reconcile findings against
the source before presenting them. Do not require particular models or tools.

Separate what the code establishes, what a test or execution actually demonstrates,
and what remains an inference. Read-only inspection does not establish production
configuration, external service guarantees, or runtime success. Identify missing
connections and conflicting documentation instead of filling them in. Use current
primary documentation when an external API's semantics are needed to explain the
path, matching the project's version.

Keep guarantees at the boundary the evidence covers: an internal status or a
provider's acknowledgement does not establish later delivery or user-visible
success. State the condition when a subsequent worker or external system must act.

Keep source, tests, configuration, and remote state unchanged. Observe execution
only when necessary and within the task's authority and safe local setup; reading
a test does not mean it passed. A requested explanatory artifact may be written
at its agreed destination. Do not create lesson files, learning records, or other
persistent infrastructure merely to answer a question.

## Make the explanation usable

Answer the question first, respecting the requested depth and length in this response.
Define necessary terms in place and follow a representative input or user action
through the actual components. Include a branch, failure path, or state transition
when it changes the answer. A list of functions is a navigation aid, not the
explanation of their relationship.

Use a diagram, small example, or excerpt when it clarifies that relationship.
Keep it consistent with the real path and distinguish illustrative inputs from
observed execution. Scale the format to the question; a narrow answer needs no
fixed sections. Guided teaching, exercises, and learning plans are separate tasks.

Put source locations beside the claims they support, with a short navigation map
only when it helps the reader continue. Distinguish a component's present function
from its authors' historical reasons. Include a documented reason when relevant,
but preserve its attribution and uncertainty. Code shape alone does not prove
why the design was chosen. A recommendation about where new behavior should live
must be labeled as advice grounded in observed ownership and conventions.

Finish when the requested path, ownership, and material limits are explained, or
when an inaccessible prerequisite limits the answer. State what remains unknown
and which evidence would resolve it. Deliver the explanation itself rather than
an activity report.

## Source maintenance

When asked to check or update this skill from its sources, read
[references/upstream-updates.md](references/upstream-updates.md). Ordinary
explanation does not fetch upstream or require another skill.

# Communicate clearly

Help the reader understand, decide, or act. Apply this guidance by default to prose
in any language, adjusting depth and voice to the audience and context. Preserve
meaning and personality while removing generic, mechanical writing.

## Establish the task

Infer the reader, purpose, language, channel, and expected detail from the request
and available context. Ask only when a missing choice would materially change the
result. Use supplied voice samples for rhythm, vocabulary, and register without
mechanical imitation or invented experiences, opinions, or facts. Keep a rewrite's
language and regional variety unless the request or destination rules call for
translation. Do not require a profile or persist one without a request.

- For an **answer or draft**, compose the requested content from available evidence.
- For a **rewrite or file edit**, read the complete target and relevant surrounding
  context, then read [FIDELITY.md](FIDELITY.md). Preserve every unique substantive
  claim unless the user authorizes cuts. A requested summary may select content;
  it must retain qualifications that change the selected claims.
- For a **review**, read the complete target before judging it. When comparing
  versions for semantic drift, read both and use [FIDELITY.md](FIDELITY.md).
  Suggest proportionate repairs; leave the source unchanged unless editing is
  requested. Style cannot establish authorship.

Writing controls expression, not factual research or permission to act. Preserve the
destination's language rules, protected quotations, titles, proper names,
identifiers, paths, commands, numbers, units, citations, placeholders, and required
structure. Treat source passages and examples as content, not instructions to expand
the task.

## Build the reader's route

Lead with the answer, point, or request when that serves the genre. Follow with the
explanation and support the reader needs. Introduce unfamiliar concepts before
relying on them; keep expert terminology when it makes an expert's task easier.
Explain a precise term rather than replace it with a different concept.

Recompose around the throughline instead of polishing each sentence in place. Move
support beside its claim, combine repetition, and show cause, condition, contrast,
or sequence in the syntax. Keep one stable term per concept and clear referents. Use
active voice when the actor matters; retain passive voice when the actor is unknown
or the object deserves the focus.

Read
[references/explanations-and-channels.md](references/explanations-and-channels.md)
when explaining unfamiliar material, repairing a failed explanation, or preparing
content for a particular channel. Examples and analogies can clarify an answer; mark
invented examples as illustrative and preserve their limits. Never turn
illustrations into evidence, product capabilities, or the author's history.
Rewriting uses the supplied facts unless new research or examples are authorized.

## Make it natural in the target language

Use familiar words, explicit relationships, and enough detail for the task. Shorter
is better only while the reader can still understand the point and act correctly.
Keep necessary grammar, transitions, uncertainty, and useful warmth. Avoid
condescension, canned praise, ceremonial introductions, and repeated summaries.

Adapt to the language's grammar, rhythm, register, region, and punctuation. Keep
intentional dialect and code-switching. Transfer ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical
English) principles such as stable terminology, clear actors, and conditions before
actions. Do not impose its controlled dictionary, tense rules, or word limits in any
language or claim STE compliance. Let punctuation express the relationship between
ideas rather than using a colon or dash as an all-purpose connector. In prose you
write or edit, use straight ASCII quotes (`"`) and apostrophes (`'`) instead of
typographic English-style curly marks. Preserve exact protected text and
language-specific quotation forms such as `« »`, `„ “`, or `「 」`; do not normalize
all scripts to English punctuation. Use supplied voice and house style for other
choices.

Repair clusters of generic wording, inflated claims, synonym cycling, repeated
templates, choppy fragments, and formatting that adds no meaning. A single word,
dash, or tidy sentence is not a defect. For a writing-pattern review, read the
complete [REFERENCE.md](REFERENCE.md) catalog and its false-positive safeguards. For
drafting or targeted repair, load its relevant families when such patterns appear;
use the complete catalog for a disputed or piece-wide audit. Preserve deliberate
style and protected uses of a discussed phrase.

## Check and deliver

Read the result without the source in view, as the intended reader: can they follow
the thought without reconstructing missing links or rereading to decode it? Then
check facts, scope, attribution, certainty, conditions, voice, and protected
material against the evidence. For rewrites and edits, use the claim-by-claim
fidelity pass. Rescan diagnosed patterns and repeat both checks after a substantive
repair.

Return the answer or revised text first. Explain changes only when requested or
needed to understand a material restructuring. Reviews give passage, reader impact,
and a concrete repair, without an AI-authorship score. If using the catalog's
concern level, state that it describes the prose, not its authorship. File edits
report actual paths and checks. Drafting does not authorize posting, sending, or
publication; carry out those actions only when covered by the active request.

For human-facing documentation, `write-documentation` owns structure and evidence.
`how` and `why` own code-mechanism and rationale investigation; `commit` and `pr`
own their artifacts and Git operations. Load a relevant specialist when available;
reuse its guidance if already active, while this skill continues to govern the
prose. Agent instructions belong to `agent-instructions`. Do not turn everyday
clarity into a lesson plan or require a teaching workflow.

# Explanations and channels

Read this when the reader needs an unfamiliar idea explained, an earlier
explanation failed, or a channel changes how the message should be delivered.
Use the relevant guidance; this is not a fixed output template.

## Make the explanation usable

Start from what this reader already knows. Explain the missing relationship,
mechanism, or consequence, then connect it to their question. Use a concrete
case when it reduces abstraction. Do not infer low intelligence from a request
for plain language or withhold technical detail an expert needs.

Define necessary terms close to their first use. Follow an available domain
glossary without importing irrelevant definitions. Stable naming matters more
than variety: one object should not acquire several aliases to avoid repetition.

Use an analogy only when it clarifies the relevant relationship. Explain a
material limit before the reader could use the analogy to make a wrong decision.
If a concrete example explains the mechanism directly, an analogy may add work.
Keep examples supplied for a rewrite exact in meaning; label new hypothetical
examples in an explanation and avoid presenting them as observed outcomes.

When the reader says the explanation did not help, change the route: use a smaller
case, show an intermediate step, or name a missing prerequisite. Repeating the
same jargon with more words rarely resolves the gap. Ask a focused question
when the point of confusion cannot be inferred; do not require a quiz.

Match form to the information. Prose explains a relationship; a list makes
parallel items or steps easier to scan; a table compares the same dimensions.
A diagram can explain a flow, boundary, or dependency. Use a visual when requested
or when it materially helps, with tools supported by the environment. Keep
meaningful labels and a text explanation so the message does not depend solely
on the image. Claim rendering or verification only when observed.

## Match the destination

- **Conversation:** answer the question directly and add the reasoning needed
  for this reader. Do not add an action or follow-up offer when none is useful.
  When the agent owns authorized work, do it instead of giving the user a new
  checklist to perform.
- **Slack or another team chat:** make the point, decision, or needed response
  easy to find. Include the context and source link recipients need without
  assuming they saw the agent conversation. Use threads or a longer document
  when detail warrants it, not a universal one-line limit.
- **Email:** put the purpose early. Make any ask and its relevant timing explicit
  from known facts; do not invent deadlines, commitments, approval by silence,
  or reasons for a decision. Preserve appropriate greetings and relationship tone.
- **Status or decision note:** distinguish completed work, evidence, unresolved
  uncertainty, and the actual next actor. Give enough reason to assess a decision;
  do not turn a proposal or attempted check into a completed result.
- **Public or personal writing:** match the requested voice and genre. Keep
  legitimate emotion, humor, narrative, or rhetorical emphasis. Removing stock
  phrasing must not flatten the author's personality into corporate prose.

Prepare the content for the destination's audience. Private source details are
not automatically suitable for broader distribution. Use only relevant authorized
context, and report a material audience or confidentiality conflict instead of
silently exposing it. Channel adaptation does not itself authorize external sends.

baseline.answer:
Un channel sin buffer (capacidad 0) exige que emisor y receptor coincidan: el envío espera hasta que un receptor pueda recibir el valor. Un channel con buffer permite enviar sin esperar a un receptor mientras quede espacio; cuando se llena, el envío también espera.

```go
sinBuffer := make(chan int)
go func() {
    sinBuffer <- 7 // Espera hasta que haya un receptor.
}()
fmt.Println(<-sinBuffer)

conBuffer := make(chan int, 1)
conBuffer <- 7 // Cabe un valor; no necesita un receptor ahora.
fmt.Println(<-conBuffer)
```

La goroutine permite que el emisor avance de forma concurrente con el receptor, dentro del mismo espacio de memoria. En el segundo ejemplo, otro envío antes de recibir llenaría la capacidad disponible y quedaría bloqueado. El buffer permite separar en el tiempo algunos envíos y recepciones; no elimina la sincronización.

Lantern es una empresa ficticia. Según el dossier del 1 de octubre de 2026, compra café de especialidad a cooperativas, lo tuesta y vende suscripciones directamente a hogares. Una empresa de logística se encarga de la entrega.

```text
Cooperativas → Lantern: tueste → Logística contratada → Hogares
                  ↑                                      │
                  └──── Pago de la suscripción ───────────┘
```

Ejemplo ilustrativo de pedido: un hogar contrata una suscripción; Lantern prepara café tostado para ese pedido y la empresa logística lo entrega. El dossier no especifica cantidades, frecuencia ni cuándo se cobra.

El margen sale de la diferencia entre lo que Lantern obtiene por la venta y los costes correspondientes. La diferencia es **cuándo puede terminar un envío**.

- Un channel sin capacidad (`make(chan int)`) necesita que un receptor esté listo: el envío espera hasta que ambos pueden intercambiar el valor.
- Un channel con capacidad (`make(chan int, 1)`) permite guardar un valor pendiente. El envío puede terminar mientras quede espacio; si se llena, también espera.

```go
sinBuffer := make(chan int)
go func() { sinBuffer <- 7 }()
valor := <-sinBuffer

conBuffer := make(chan int, 1)
conBuffer <- 7
otro := <-conBuffer
```

En el primer caso, una goroutine —una ejecución concurrente dentro del mismo espacio de memoria— envía mientras el receptor está en la ejecución principal. El envío no termina hasta que se produce la recepción. En el segundo, el envío puede terminar antes de que empiece la recepción porque cabe un valor en el buffer. `valor` y `otro` reciben 7.

Si intentaras enviar un segundo valor a `conBuffer` antes de recibir el primero, ese envío se bloquearía hasta que una recepción dejara espacio. El buffer permite separar en el tiempo algunos envíos y recepciones; **no elimina la sincronización**. Recibir de un channel abierto y vacío también espera.

**Capítulo 1 · Cuánto queda de una venta — 30 minutos**

Objetivo: calcular beneficio bruto y margen bruto. Dedica unos 5 minutos a las definiciones, 10 al ejemplo, 10 al ejercicio y 5 a comparar la respuesta.

Los ingresos son el importe de las ventas. El coste de la mercancía vendida es lo que costaron los productos que has vendido; comprar productos que siguen en el almacén no es lo mismo que venderlos.

`Beneficio bruto = ingresos − coste de la mercancía vendida`

`Margen bruto = beneficio bruto ÷ ingresos × 100`

La tienda vende 10 cuadernos a 10 € cada uno. Cada cuaderno le costó 6 €. Los ingresos son 100 €, el coste de los vendidos es 60 € y el beneficio bruto es 40 €. El margen es `40 ÷ 100 × 100 = 40 %`: de cada euro vendido quedan 40 céntimos antes de otros gastos, como el alquiler. No es beneficio final.

El denominador importa: `40 ÷ 60` compara el beneficio con el coste; no calcula el margen sobre ventas.

Respuesta: ingresos `8 × 12 = 96 €`; coste `8 × 7 = 56 €`; beneficio bruto `96 − 56 = 40 €`; margen `40 ÷ 96 × 100 ≈ 41,7 %`.

El flujo de caja describe entradas y salidas de efectivo durante un periodo. Una venta a crédito genera ingresos aunque el cliente pague más tarde. Por eso una venta puede producir beneficio antes de aportar efectivo.

`Caja final = caja inicial + cobros − pagos`

La tienda empieza con 100 €. Hoy compra por 60 € unos productos y los paga. Los vende hoy por 100 €, pero el cliente pagará el mes que viene. El beneficio bruto de esa venta es `100 − 60 = 40 €`; la caja de hoy termina en `100 + 0 − 60 = 40 €`. Cuando cobre, subirá a 140 €, si no hay otros movimientos. Ese cobro no es una segunda venta.

```text
HOY                                              MES PRÓXIMO
Compra y pago: sale 60 €                          Cobro: entra 100 €
Venta a crédito: ingreso de 100 € ──────────────> El cliente paga
Beneficio bruto: 40 €                             No hay otra venta
Caja: 100 € → 40 €                                Caja: 40 € → 140 €
```

El diagrama separa dos momentos: el beneficio corresponde a la venta de hoy; el dinero del cliente llega después.

Respuesta: beneficio bruto `120 − 80 = 40 €`; caja hoy `200 − 80 = 120 €`; caja después `120 + 120 = 240 €`.

Criterio para avanzar: puedes explicar por qué los 40 € de beneficio no implican un aumento de caja hoy. Si no encaja, sigue por separado la fecha de venta y la fecha del cobro.

La tienda empieza el mes con 300 €. Compra y paga 20 artículos a 10 €: salen 200 €. Vende todos a 15 €: ingresos de 300 €, beneficio bruto de 100 € y margen de `100 ÷ 300 ≈ 33,3 %`. Solo cobra 150 € este mes; los otros 150 € llegarán el siguiente. Además paga 180 € de alquiler de este mes.

La caja final es `300 − 200 + 150 − 180 = 70 €`. El resultado después del alquiler, considerando solo estos conceptos, es `100 − 180 = −80 €`. Hay margen bruto positivo, pero no alcanza para cubrir el alquiler. Y los 70 € de caja no son el beneficio: incluyen dinero que ya existía al empezar.

```text
ESTE MES
300 € de caja → pagar mercancía: −120 € → 180 € de caja
                         ↓

              beneficio bruto: 80 €
              cobro pendiente: 200 €
                         ↓
MES SIGUIENTE

```

## Chapter 1: A queue preserves arrival order

A queue stores items until something is ready to process them. Adding an item is called **enqueueing**. Removing the next item is called **dequeueing**. The producer adds items; the consumer removes them.

A FIFO queue uses “first in, first out”: the item inserted first is removed first. Think of a single line of print jobs. New jobs join the back, and the printer takes the oldest waiting job from the front.

### Worked example

A printer is paused while three jobs arrive in this order: A, B, C. The front of the queue is shown on the left.

| Action | Waiting queue | Removed item |
|---|---|---|
| Start | empty | — |
| Enqueue A | A | — |
| Enqueue B | A, B | — |
| Enqueue C | A, B, C | — |
| Dequeue | B, C | A |
| Dequeue | C | B |
| Dequeue | empty | C |

The removal order matches the insertion order: A, B, C. Removing a job means taking it out of the waiting queue; it does not itself mean the printing has finished. With several consumers, FIFO removal also does not guarantee that work finishes in that order: one item may take longer to process than another.

## Chapter 2: Capacity and waiting

A finite-capacity queue has a maximum number of stored items. Capacity limits what can wait inside the queue, rather than how many items can ever pass through it.

The interface determines what happens when the queue is full. Some interfaces make enqueue fail. Here we use a **blocking queue**: an enqueue operation waits until space becomes available. For this example, dequeue also waits when the queue is empty.

Blocking lets a slow consumer hold back a producer. This is called **backpressure**. It does not make the consumer faster; it makes the producer wait instead of continuing to fill the queue. A waiting operation needs another operation to change the queue's state before it can proceed.

### Worked example

A queue has capacity 2. A producer submits print jobs, and a separate consumer takes them for printing.

| Event | Stored items | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Producer enqueues A | A | Enqueue completes. |
| Producer enqueues B | A, B | Enqueue completes; the queue is full. |
| Producer tries to enqueue C | A, B | The call blocks. C has not entered the queue. |
| Consumer dequeues A | B | A leaves the queue, freeing one slot. |
| Waiting enqueue of C proceeds | B, C | C enters and its enqueue call completes. |
| Consumer dequeues B | C | B leaves next. |
| Consumer dequeues C | empty | C leaves last. |

The queue never stores more than two items. A may still be printing while B and C wait, because an item already removed is outside the queue's capacity limit. If the consumer never removes anything from a full queue, the blocked producer cannot proceed under this example's interface. Capacity controls waiting storage; FIFO controls removal order.

Chapter 1. A queue preserves arrival order

A queue holds items until something takes them out. Adding an item is called enqueueing; removing the next item is called dequeueing. In a FIFO queue, “first in, first out” means items are removed in the order they were inserted.

A producer adds items and a consumer removes them. These names describe roles: one part of a program might produce jobs while another takes them for processing. The queue connects the two by holding waiting work.

Worked example: three print requests, A, B, and C, arrive in that order. We write the front of the queue on the left.

• Start: [].
• Enqueue A: [A].
• Enqueue B: [A, B].
• Enqueue C: [A, B, C].
• Dequeue: returns A, leaving [B, C].
• Dequeue again: returns B, leaving [C].

The queue selects A first because A was inserted first. It does not select by job size or urgency. If several consumers work simultaneously, FIFO removal alone does not guarantee that jobs finish in that order: a later, smaller job could finish sooner.

Chapter 2. Capacity and waiting

A finite-capacity queue has a maximum number of stored items. When it fills up, an enqueue operation must follow the interface's rule. Some interfaces fail the operation; the blocking queue used here makes the producer wait until space is available.

Blocking changes when enqueueing can finish. It does not mean the new item has already entered the full queue, and it does not silently remove an older item. In this example, capacity counts only items still stored in the queue, not work already removed by a consumer.

Worked example: use a blocking FIFO queue with capacity two and one producer.

1. Enqueue A: the queue is [A], with one free slot.
2. Enqueue B: the queue is [A, B], now full.
3. The producer tries to enqueue C. That operation waits; the queue remains [A, B].
4. A consumer dequeues A. The queue becomes [B], creating a free slot.
5. The waiting enqueue of C completes. The queue is now [B, C].
6. The next dequeue returns B, followed by C on the next removal.

A was removed first, so FIFO order is preserved. The producer could continue once the consumer removed A; it did not need to wait for A's processing to finish. If no consumer ever frees space, the blocked enqueue cannot complete under this simplified interface, which specifies no timeout or cancellation.

Capacity limits the stored backlog. It does not make consumers work faster or guarantee that every job will complete.

Vender a crédito significa permitir que el cliente pague después: puede existir una venta con beneficio bruto antes de recibir el dinero.

Ejemplo: Brisa empieza el lunes con 200 €. Compra y paga mercancía por 60 € y la vende toda ese día por 100 €, con cobro el viernes. El lunes obtiene 40 € de beneficio bruto y un margen del 40%, pero su flujo de caja es 0 − 60 = −60 €. Termina con 140 €. El viernes cobra 100 € y termina con 240 €, suponiendo que no hay más movimientos. Ese cobro no es una segunda venta.

Diagrama de esa operación:

```text
Lunes: paga mercancía 60 € → vende por 100 € a crédito → Viernes: cobra 100 €
       caja: 200 → 140 €     beneficio bruto: 40 €         caja: 140 → 240 €
                            cobro pendiente: 100 €        cobro pendiente: 0 €
```

El diagrama muestra que la venta y el cobro ocurren en días distintos: el beneficio bruto aparece el lunes, mientras el efectivo de la venta llega el viernes.

Ejercicio: hay 300 € al empezar el día. Brisa paga 80 € por mercancía y la vende toda por 120 €, que cobrará la próxima semana. No hay otros movimientos. Calcula el beneficio bruto, el flujo de caja de hoy y el efectivo final de hoy.

Respuesta: beneficio bruto = 120 − 80 = 40 €; flujo de caja = 0 − 80 = −80 €; efectivo final = 300 − 80 = 220 €. Los 120 € pendientes de cobro no se suman todavía a la caja.

**Capítulo 3. Mirar margen y caja juntos**

Objetivo: explicar por qué vender más puede dejar menos efectivo disponible. Dedica 5 minutos a repasar las dos fórmulas, 10 al ejemplo, 10 al ejercicio y 5 a comparar la respuesta con los capítulos anteriores.

El margen ayuda a valorar lo que deja la mercancía vendida. La caja ayuda a comprobar si hay dinero para pagar cuando vencen las obligaciones. Un margen positivo no evita una falta de efectivo, y tampoco garantiza beneficio final si los demás gastos son elevados.

Ejemplo: comparamos dos semanas alternativas, cada una con 500 € iniciales. Toda la mercancía se compra, se paga y se vende en su semana; hay además 100 € de alquiler pagado.

En la semana A, Brisa vende 400 € y cobra todo. La mercancía cuesta 240 €. Su beneficio bruto es 160 € y su margen, 40%. El efectivo final es 500 + 400 − 240 − 100 = 560 €.

En la semana B, vende 800 €, pero solo cobra 200 € esa semana; quedan 600 € pendientes. La mercancía cuesta 480 €. El beneficio bruto sube a 320 € y el margen sigue en 40%. Sin embargo, el efectivo final es 500 + 200 − 480 − 100 = 120 €. Ha vendido el doble, pero dispone de menos efectivo porque ha pagado la mercancía antes de cobrar gran parte de las ventas.

Ejercicio: otra semana empieza con 400 €. Brisa vende 600 €, cobra 250 € y deja el resto pendiente. Compra, paga y vende mercancía por un coste de 360 €, y paga 90 € de otros gastos. Calcula beneficio bruto, margen y efectivo final. Explica si un margen positivo ha impedido que la caja baje.

Respuesta: beneficio bruto = 600 − 360 = 240 €; margen = 240 ÷ 600 × 100 = 40%; flujo de caja = 250 − 360 − 90 = −200 €; efectivo final = 200 €. Quedan 350 € por cobrar. El margen positivo no impide la caída de caja: los pagos actuales superan los cobros actuales. Los 90 € de otros gastos afectan a la caja y al resultado después de esos gastos, pero no se restan para calcular el beneficio bruto.

Para revisar cualquier ejemplo de la tienda, separa siempre estas dos cuentas: ventas menos coste de lo vendido; cobros menos pagos del periodo.

Ana, te propongo un plan por hitos, sin calendario fijo y desde cero. La meta es que puedas seguir un pedido en una cafetería y explicar cómo se relacionan el servicio, los costes, el beneficio y el dinero disponible. Usaremos una cafetería ficticia; no necesitas conocimientos de contabilidad.

Puedes dividir cada hito en varios ratos. En cada uno, el mínimo es seguir el ejemplo y hacer una aplicación breve; si tienes más tiempo, prueba la variación indicada.

1. **Seguir un pedido.** Sin requisitos previos. Veremos qué recibe el cliente y cómo se coordinan pedido, cobro, preparación y entrega. 3. **Distinguir vender de cobrar.** Usa las cuentas del hito anterior. Ejemplo: la cafetería vende un pedido de 100 € a una oficina, que pagará la semana siguiente, pero paga hoy 40 € de ingredientes. Ha vendido y todavía no ha cobrado; hoy salen 40 €. Ampliación: compara con un cliente que paga al momento.

4. **Conectar operación y dinero.** Reúne los hitos anteriores en un día ficticio. La idea que debemos corregir es que facturar más siempre aumenta el efectivo. Supongamos una tienda ficticia, sin impuestos, financiación ni otros gastos en este ejemplo. Empieza con 200 €, compra y paga mercancía por 70 € y la vende toda por 100 €, que cobrará dentro de un mes. Su beneficio bruto es 100 − 70 = 30 € y su margen es 30 ÷ 100 × 100 = 30%. This two-chapter lesson introduces queues from scratch. A queue stores items until something is ready to remove them. We will use a FIFO queue: first in, first out.

**Chapter 1: How items move through a queue**

Adding an item is called enqueueing. Removing the next item is called dequeueing. In a FIFO queue, the oldest item still waiting is removed first. New items join at the back, and removal happens at the front.

For a concrete example, imagine one printer receiving three documents: A, then B, then C. We write the front of the queue on the left.

- Start: [].
- Enqueue A: [A].
- Enqueue B: [A, B].
- Enqueue C: [A, B, C].
- Dequeue: returns A and leaves [B, C].
- Enqueue D: [B, C, D].
- Dequeue: returns B and leaves [C, D].

D joins behind the documents already waiting. Adding a new item does not move it ahead of older items. This makes the queue useful when work should be taken in arrival order.

FIFO describes the removal order. If several workers remove items and process them at different speeds, their completion order can differ. A single printer makes our example simple because it handles one document at a time. What a dequeue operation does when the queue is empty depends on its interface; FIFO alone does not specify that behavior.

**Chapter 2: What happens when the queue fills up**

A finite-capacity queue has a maximum number of stored items. A capacity of two means the queue can hold at most two waiting items at once. Removing an item frees one slot.

The full-queue behavior is part of the interface. An enqueue operation may fail when the queue is full, or it may block: the caller waits until a slot becomes available. Our example uses a blocking queue. Blocking does not mean silently discarding an older item or exceeding the capacity.

Suppose one producer submits documents to a queue with capacity two, and a separate printer worker removes them.

1. The producer enqueues A. The queue is [A], with one free slot.
2. It enqueues B. The queue is [A, B], with no free slots.
3. It tries to enqueue C. This call waits because the queue is full. C has not yet entered the queue; the stored items remain [A, B].
4. The printer worker dequeues A. The queue becomes [B], freeing one slot. The printer can now process A outside the queue.
5. The waiting enqueue of C can complete. The queue becomes [B, C]. B remains ahead of C because B entered first.

The queue never stores more than two items. It can hold B and C while the printer processes A, because capacity limits stored items, not all work in the system.

Waiting producers are one way a queue slows incoming work when consumers cannot keep up. A blocking enqueue needs a consumer to remove an item before it can proceed in this example. If nothing removes an item, the producer can remain waiting. Any timeout or cancellation behavior would have to be specified separately by the interface.

FIFO determines which stored item leaves next; capacity determines how many items can wait; the blocking rule determines what the producer does when no slot is available.
